extracted.intended_audience: military officers, post commanders, judge advocates, and other military legal practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and regulatory standards governing the authority, duties, and limits of commanding officers (post/transport/regimental/company) including arrest, confinement, jurisdiction, delegation of authority, and related procedural obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of suspension sentence on confinement
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence of suspension from duty and pay for 15 days does not imply confinement to quarters, or involve a condition of arrest; customarily an officer undergoing such suspension is allowed the limits of his command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that suspension from duty/pay is not equivalent to confinement; customary practice allows freedom within command limits. (R. 7, 242, Feb., 1864.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander authority over soldiers marrying
rubrics_metrics.description: A military commander authorized to grant or refuse passes or furloughs may refuse permission to leave the post to a soldier whose purpose is to become married; commander may exclude wives from a post for discipline reasons; however there is no statute or regulation forbidding soldiers from contracting marriage while in service, and the act of marrying is not per se a military offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If marriage involves neglect of duty or disorder, soldier may be tried for that conduct but not for marrying as such. If marrying after enlistment becomes generally demoralizing, only Congress can remedy by legislation. (R. 38, 47, Apr., 1876; 407, Jan., 1877; 43, 109, Dec., 1879.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander may set off-duty limits forbidding certain places
rubrics_metrics.description: A post commander who issues an order allowing soldiers 'off duty' limits extending one mile beyond the reservation and forbidding them to enter or patronize gambling houses, saloons, etc., does not exceed his authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports reasonable regulation of off-duty conduct within defined limits to preserve discipline. (C. 1210, Apr., 1895.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil arrest on bail does not alter military duty/pay status
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier arrested by civil authorities and released on bail to await trial may, on returning to his station, be required to perform the usual military duty appropriate to his rank, and while on such duty his pay status is unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil process does not automatically change military obligations or pay unless otherwise ordered. (R. 24, 279, Feb., 1867; C. 1717, Sept., 1895.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander ordering to duty a soldier excused by surgeon
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the post commander may order to duty a soldier excused from duty by the surgeon for sickness or disability, if he does so he assumes responsibility for any material injury that may result and is amenable to trial for any military offense involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commander who overrides medical excuse bears responsibility for adverse consequences. (R. 43, 250, Mar., 1880.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Return of money wrongfully turned over by commander
rubrics_metrics.description: If at arrest money is found on a soldier and that money is turned over by the post commander to a trader who claims it, and the soldier is later tried and acquitted, the post commander should refund the amount taken from the soldier and improperly turned over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post commanders must not improperly transfer or retain private property found on soldiers; restitution required when seizure/turnover was improper. (R. 50, 520, July, 1886.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of converted proceeds found on convicted soldier
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier obtained money by false pretenses and converted it into other denominations, and the unexpended balance was found on his person at arrest, the sum taken should be returned to the victim from whom it had been obtained by false pretenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when money on person is of different denominations, courts may require return to victim if traceable as proceeds of the offense. (C. 233 W, May 29, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of excluding persons from post grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A post commander can in his discretion exclude all persons other than those belonging to his post from post and reservation grounds; but admitting everybody except one individual against whom no charge exists would be an abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretion to control access must be exercised fairly and not arbitrarily. (C. 2682, Oct., 1896; multiple citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Post cannot be asylum for fugitives from civil justice
rubrics_metrics.description: A post commander cannot properly allow his post to become an asylum for fugitives from civil justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military reservations should not be used to shield civilians from lawful civil process. (R. 36, 450, May, 1875.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When military personnel may arrest civilians without warrant
rubrics_metrics.description: A civilian may be arrested without a warrant by a military person as by any citizen where he commits a felony or crime in breach of the public peace in such person's presence, or where, after a felony, there is probable cause to believe the party is the felon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On arrest at a military post, arresting officer should use no unnecessary violence, disclose official character, inform cause of arrest, and deliver the party as soon as reasonably practicable to a civil official authorized to hold and bring him before a magistrate. (P. 39, 51, Feb., 1890; other citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest authority on ceded federal jurisdiction lands
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a State has ceded exclusive jurisdiction to the United States over a federal installation, the commanding officer or his subordinates may arrest offenders without warrant within authorized limits and must bring them before the specified federal official; if no such official accessible, may hold offender in guardhouse only for necessary interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal control on ceded lands carries arrest and temporary detention authority but requires prompt presentation to federal judicial officers. (P. 39, 51, Feb., 1890.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Superintendent of Military Academy and civilian arrests
rubrics_metrics.description: The superintendent of the Military Academy is not generally authorized to arrest and confine a civilian in the guardhouse for a mere breach of police regulations; proper remedy is removal of the offender as soon as practicable without unnecessary force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of confinement against civilians for minor regulatory breaches is improper; prefer removal and minimal force. (P. 41, 457, July, 1890; other citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of soldier's spouse from post for cause
rubrics_metrics.description: A post commander can legally order the removal of a soldier's wife from the post for sufficient cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commanders may remove non-military persons from post when justified by discipline or cause. (C. 25177, July 14, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Search warrant required for suspected civilian possession of uniform clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Although possession of uniform clothing is presumptive evidence of sale under section 3748 R.S., where there is reason to believe such clothing is in possession of a citizen, a search warrant should be obtained from the proper United States court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects civilian property rights; use judicial process for searches. (C. 5308, Nov. 22, 1898; other citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of shore and waters adjacent to military reservation
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of cession of exclusive jurisdiction for military purposes, grant includes necessary easement in the shore and adjacent waters required for free use and enjoyment; post commander should exercise control of shore between high and low water marks to prevent occupation interfering with military use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing public fishing rights with necessary military easements; commander to prevent occupations incompatible with military use. (C. 19657, Oct. 21, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutting grass on reservation may constitute theft
rubrics_metrics.description: Grass cut for hay upon a military reservation, if not removed promptly, may be treated as personal property; a person wrongfully cutting it and allowing it to remain until hay could be made may be chargeable with stealing United States property under the act of March 3, 1875.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unauthorized appropriation of natural resources on reservation can be felony punishable by fine and imprisonment. (P. 64, 270, 303, Mar. and Apr., 1894.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to refer cases to a general court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a general court-martial has been convened at a post by the department commander, the post commander is not empowered, absent authority from such superior, to refer cases to the court for trial; such action is irregular and a transcending of his province.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits on convening/referral authority preserve proper chain of command. (R. 41, 306, July, 1878.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Post commander acting as counsel for prisoners discouraged
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation providing for the detail by the commander of a post at which a general court-martial is ordered to sit of a suitable officer to act as counsel for prisoners if requested is not to be construed as sanctioning the post commander voluntarily appearing as counsel at his own post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids conflict of interest; post commander should not act as defense counsel at his own post. (P. 65, 77, May, 1894.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty in response to writ of habeas corpus by U.S. courts
rubrics_metrics.description: When a writ of habeas corpus is issued by the United States judiciary for a person held in military custody, it is the duty of the officer to whom the writ is addressed to make a full return of the facts and to bring the body into court, submitting the whole question of authority and discharge and abiding by the court's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full factual return and production of the person are required when the writ is from a coordinate federal judiciary; officer must abide by the court's order. (R. 19, 377; C. 14042, Sept. 23, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts lack authority to discharge persons held by U.S. military
rubrics_metrics.description: Independently of presidential proclamations, on constitutional grounds no State court or judge can discharge, on habeas corpus, a person held in military custody by authority of the United States; State courts have no jurisdiction to discharge soldiers arrested or confined by military authorities for desertion or to pass upon legality of enlistment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal military custody supersedes State habeas relief in these circumstances; supported by numerous precedents (Tarble's Case and others). (Multiple citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to State habeas writ served on military officer
rubrics_metrics.description: When a writ of habeas corpus issued by a State court is served on a military officer, he is not required to produce the body; it is sufficient to make a return showing clearly that the person is held by authority of the United States as a deserter, under enlistment, or otherwise; the State court will properly dismiss the writ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military officers may rely on a factual return rather than production when subject to State process; prior practice included resisting State contempt orders (pre-Tarble). (R. 3, 104; 21, 157.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to State court enforcement pre-Tarble
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to Tarble's decision, if a State court attempted to enforce contempt or discharge against an officer who refused to produce the body after making a return showing federal custody, such attempt should be resisted and the officer supported by necessary military force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice asserting federal supremacy in such conflicts (pre-Tarble jurisprudence). (R. 3, 502; 19, 305; etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Military re-arrest after improper State discharge pre-Tarble
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a State court discharged an officer undergoing a court-martial or a soldier was discharged by a State court on enlistment grounds prior to Tarble, the military authorities were advised to re-arrest and reconfine or rearrest and hold to service as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms military remedy to restore custody where State interference occurred (historical practice). (R. 30, 56; C. 14042; other citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for deaths on reservations vs. outside
rubrics_metrics.description: If officers/enlisted men or civilians die on reservations under circumstances presenting no question of violation of State laws, an investigation by a board of officers or court of inquiry suffices; but if death occurs outside reservation limits or results from crimes committed outside, the coroner's right to conduct an inquest is plain and the post commander should not obstruct the inquest or removal of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect comity with civil authorities for deaths involving state jurisdiction; limit military inquests when civil jurisdiction is proper. (C. 20050, July 13, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Furnishing guardhouse to civil authorities in emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: A commanding officer may, in emergencies, furnish guardhouse accommodations on request of the civil authorities for safekeeping of civilian prisoners, provided the men charged with safekeeping are furnished by the civil authorities, as there is no authority for employment of troops for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military may assist by providing space but not by using troops to guard civilians unless civil authorities supply guard personnel. (C. 25768, Nov. 9, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer on Army transport may be placed on duty and receive allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer returning from leave on an Army transport may lawfully be placed on duty by the commanding officer of the troops on board, and while so engaged becomes entitled to the allowances accruing to officers on duty while traveling by sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travel status and allowances apply when an officer is placed on duty aboard transport. (C. 24362, Jan. 19, 1909; July 13, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Military prosecution for offenses on Army transport (subject to Articles of War)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an offense is committed on an Army transport by a person subject to the Articles of War, military prosecution should be initiated at once by preparation of charges and specifications and by notifying the person that military jurisdiction has attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt initiation of military criminal process required when military jurisdiction attaches on transport. (C. 5635, Oct. 31, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender of offender from transport in territorial waters against civilian
rubrics_metrics.description: If an offense is committed on an Army transport in the territorial waters of a State or Territory against a civilian, the offender will be surrendered upon presentation of a warrant by the proper Federal, State, or Territorial authority; the officer serving the warrant will receive necessary assistance as in the 59th article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When civil jurisdiction applies in territorial waters, officers must comply with valid civil process and assist execution. (C. 5635, Oct. 31, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of serious offenses on high seas among ship personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: When a felony or serious misdemeanor is committed on the high seas by one member of a transport company against another and neither is subject to the Articles of War, the offender will be confined and turned over to the proper United States court at the first port of entry; if no such court at the port, hold aboard until an appropriate port is reached. If in territorial waters, turn over to proper State/Territorial court. Lesser infractions may receive disciplinary punishment by the ship's master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between high sea jurisdiction and territorial waters; provides fallback when federal court unavailable and allows shipboard discipline for minor offenses. (C. 5635, Oct. 31, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority in surrender when multiple warrants issued
rubrics_metrics.description: If warrants from a United States court and from a State or Territorial court issue in the same case, the commanding officer of a transport will surrender the offender to the officer whose service is first in point of time; no officer of the Army will undertake to pass upon sufficiency of a warrant issued by any such court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive officers must respect temporal priority of warrants and avoid judicial determinations of warrant sufficiency. (C. 5635, Oct. 31, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport quartermaster succession to command
rubrics_metrics.description: A transport quartermaster not serving by detail as an officer of the Quartermaster's Department succeeds to command of troops on board if he is the senior officer present; if he has been detailed for service in the Quartermaster's Department, he becomes a staff officer and is not entitled to exercise command in that operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status (detail vs. not detailed) affects whether quartermaster may assume command aboard transport. (G. 17508, Nov. 27, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary rank and command rights on transport
rubrics_metrics.description: A captain in the line of the Army serving by appointment as assistant chief of the Philippines Constabulary with temporary rank of colonel, though entitled to benefits of rank, is not entitled to assume or be lawfully assigned command of troops on an Army transport upon which he is traveling as a passenger; his right is measured by relevant statute requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary rank does not automatically confer command rights aboard transport unless statute permits. (C. 17508, Feb. 15, 1905.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of authority to 'appoint' regimental staff officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Army Regulations' authority to 'appoint' regimental staff officers is not part of the constitutional appointing power but is merely an authority to select and detail; such appointments may be regulated by War Department orders (e.g., restricting dates of effect or retroactive pay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary of War may regulate administrative appointment practices to protect service interests. (R. 41, 609, July, 1879; 142, 567, Apr., 1880.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for battalion staff appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Regulations give battalion commanders the right to recommend officers for appointment to vacancies in the battalion staff; regimental commanders must consider recommendations but retain discretion to disapprove for public reasons; attachment to another battalion doesn't automatically exclude a recommended officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation is influential but not dispositive; regimental commander exercises considered discretion. (C. 13292; C. 9052.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regimental commander discretion over company promotions
rubrics_metrics.description: A regimental commander is not obliged by Army Regulations to appoint as sergeants or corporals the soldiers recommended by company commanders; he has discretion and should decline appointments where he believes the nominee unfit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralizes final authority at regimental level, permitting oversight to ensure fitness for NCO ranks. (R. 27, 159, Sept., 1868.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on reduction of NCOs by regimental commander
rubrics_metrics.description: A regimental commander is without authority to reduce a company noncommissioned officer without the recommendation of the company commander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects company commander prerogative in reductions; ensures proper recommendation channels. (C. 10056, Mar. 27, 1901.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation to NCOs to confine or arrest enlisted men
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom permits a company or detachment commander to delegate to a noncommissioned officer the right to confine an enlisted man or place him in arrest in quarters where it is impossible to obtain prior order, provided the case is immediately reported to the proper commander who must confirm and adopt the act if the enlisted man is to remain confined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation is customary but not based on positive grant in the 24th article of war; confirmation by proper commander required to validate confinement. (C. 18878, Dec. 9, 1905.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy objection to broad delegation of complaint intake to NCOs
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegating to a noncommissioned officer the initial entertaining of complaints and requests of men, though not expressly prohibited, is at variance with principles of military organization and tends to render commissioned officers negligent and NCOs arbitrary and overbearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses policy/supervisory concern: while convenient sometimes, broad delegation should be restrained to protect responsibility and proper officer oversight. (Indorsement of Judge Advocate General quoting Brig. Gen. Ord; R. 42, 273, May, 1879.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Company commander and handling of soldiers' private funds
rubrics_metrics.description: A company commander cannot legally force a soldier to deposit money with the paymaster, nor, without the soldier's consent, deposit private money of the soldier which is in the commander’s possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects soldiers' autonomy over private funds and limits commander control. (R. 39, 471, Mar. 4, 1878.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Company commander's liability for bailment of money
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier's deposit of money with his company commander constitutes a bailment and probably more than a gratuitous one; if the commander delivers the money without authority to an unauthorized person (e.g., successor), even without wrongful intent, it constitutes conversion and the bailee remains liable; turning money over to successor at relief is imprudent if soldier present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commanders must exercise reasonable care with entrusted funds; improper transfers create liability. (C. 14332, Mar. 9, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel allowances when ordered on duty by special command
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer ordered to travel on duty by a special command (independently of department commander) is entitled to the usual travel allowances equally as if ordered by a department commander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orders from properly constituted special commands carry same travel allowance entitlements as departmental orders. (P. 57, 357, Jan., 1893.)
